steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a software engineering paper that presents DyPyBench, our benchmark of executable Python projects for dynamic analysis. Motivate why Python needs such a benchmark, describe its key properties, summarize the three usage scenarios we evaluate, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Python's popularity and dynamic nature
- Dynamic analyses for Python and benchmark suites in other languages
- The gap: no executable benchmark for Python
- DyPyBench and its four properties
- Three usage scenarios
- Contributions

  - find programming errors, security vulnerabilities, performance bottlenecks
  - other languages have executable benchmark suites: DaCapo for Java (cite), SPEC CPU for C/C++ (cite), Da Capo con Scala (cite)
- The gap
  - no equivalent suite for Python -> hinders dynamic analysis progress/evaluation
  - researchers must build own set of executable programs, significant effort
  - small evaluations: nine projects (cite), five (cite), six (cite), eleven (cite)
  - each team has own benchmark -> hard to compare

  - large-scale: 50 projects, 681k lines of code, order of magnitude larger than previous evaluations
  - diverse: projects systematically sampled from different application domains
  - ready-to-run: projects set up, test suites as inputs, single-command unified interface, Docker image for reproducibility/longevity

  - (1) static vs dynamic call graphs; compare to state-of-the-art static generator (cite); strengths/weaknesses, guidelines

  - usefulness shown in three scenarios

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Python has grown a lot in the last years and is now one of the most used programming languages in many fields, for example machine learning, data analysis and web applications. Python is also dynamic, it allows dynamic type checking and changing the structure of objects at runtime, and this makes it even more appealing to developers.

Other popular languages have benchmark suites of executable code that help to develop, evaluate and compare dynamic analyses. Researchers who want to work on a new dynamic analysis for Python, or who want to study the runtime behavior of Python code, or who want to collect data from executions of Python software, have to spend a lot of effort to create a suitable set of executable programs. Because of this, many evaluations of dynamic analyses for Python use a fairly small set of benchmark programs, e.g., nine projects, five projects, six projects, and eleven projects. Also, every team working on Python creates its own benchmark, so it is hard to compare the different techniques and results with each other.

- DyPyBench: new benchmark of executable Python projects, first with four properties

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Python has grown a lot in the last years and is now one of the most used programming languages in many fields, for example machine learning, data analysis and web applications. A 2022 report about the programming languages used in projects on GitHub lists Python as the second-most popular language of all. The reasons for Python's success are its simplicity, its flexibility and its large collection of libraries and frameworks. Python is also dynamic, it allows dynamic type checking and changing the structure of objects at runtime, and this makes it even more appealing to developers.

But the dynamic nature of Python also makes things hard for program analysis, error detection, security assessment and performance optimization. Many dynamic program analysis techniques were developed for these challenges, for example to detect bugs, to enforce differential privacy, to slice programs, or to understand the performance of a program with profiling. These techniques are very important for finding programming errors, security vulnerabilities and performance bottlenecks. Other popular languages have benchmark suites of executable code that help to develop, evaluate and compare dynamic analyses. For example there is DaCapo for Java, SPEC CPU for C/C++ and Da Capo con Scala, and they contributed a lot to the work of both researchers and practitioners on these languages.

Python is popular and important, but there is no equivalent benchmark suite for Python right now, and this hinders the progress and evaluation of dynamic analyses. Researchers who want to work on a new dynamic analysis for Python, or who want to study the runtime behavior of Python code, or who want to collect data from executions of Python software, have to spend a lot of effort to create a suitable set of executable programs. Because of this, many evaluations of dynamic analyses for Python use a fairly small set of benchmark programs, e.g., nine projects, five projects, six projects, and eleven projects. Also, every team working on Python creates its own benchmark, so it is hard to compare the different techniques and results with each other.

To fill this gap, this paper presents DyPyBench, a new benchmark of executable Python projects. We want our benchmark to make future work on dynamic analysis of Python easier. For this, the benchmark is the first one that has four important properties, which are large-scale, diverse, ready-to-run, and ready-to-analyze:

- • Large-scale. The benchmark should give users a big collection of executable code, so it includes a substantial number of popular and non-trivial projects. What "large-scale" means can depend on the use case. In this work we curated a dataset of 50 projects with 681k lines of code in total. This is an order of magnitude larger than the benchmarks used in the previous evaluations listed above.

- • Diverse. Python has many applications, so a benchmark must cover many application domains, and each domain has its own code style and libraries. DyPyBench tries to represent how broad and diverse Python usage is by including projects that are systematically sampled from different application domains. This enables extensive assessments and studies of code behavior in different contexts.

- • Ready-to-run. Running the code of a real-world, complex project is not trivial, because it needs a suitable project configuration, third-party dependencies installed, and inputs that exercise the code. Setting up projects can take a lot of effort, especially for users who don't know the project, and usually this effort has to be spent again for every new project. In DyPyBench all projects are already set up and the test suites of the projects are used to provide inputs. DyPyBench also provides a unified interface so users can run the benchmark with a single command, no matter how the project dependencies, configurations and execution environments differ. We also provide a Docker image with the benchmark and all its dependencies, which ensures reproducibility and longevity.

- • Ready-to-analyze. To make dynamic analysis of the projects in DyPyBench easier, the benchmark is integrated with DynaPyt, which is a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework for Python. With this integration projects can be instrumented and analyzed with a single command, so it is straightforward to apply a new dynamic analysis to many projects.

To evaluate if DyPyBench is useful and practical, we do a series of experiments covering a wide range of research areas. We apply our benchmark in three usage scenarios:

- (1) We use DyPyBench to compare statically and dynamically created call graphs empirically. We use the dynamic analysis infrastructure that is built into DyPyBench to gather dynamic call graphs and we compare them to the results of a state of the art static call graph generator. The results help to understand the strengths and weaknesses of both approaches, and give some guidelines for future work on call graph construction.

- (2) We use DyPyBench to create training data for LExecutor, which is a recent neural network-based technique for learning-guided execution. Here we apply the source code instrumentation tool that LExecutor already provides to the code in DyPyBench and then we execute our benchmark. We use the resulting 436,355 data examples as training data for the LExecutor model, and we find that more data helps to improve the accuracy of the model.

- (3) Finally, we use DyPyBench to mine specifications from execution traces. Here we again use the dynamic analysis support built into the benchmark, this time to extract traces of function calls. DyPyBench gave thousands of sequences of calls, and from them some meaningful patterns could be extracted, which sets a baseline for future work on dynamic specification mining for Python.

For all three applications, normally one would have to spend a lot of effort on setting up suitable projects and finding inputs to exercise their code, e.g., test suites. DyPyBench provides this setup instead, and this makes these and future dynamic analyses for Python much easier.

In summary our work contributes the following:

- • We create DyPyBench to address the lack of a comprehensive benchmark suite of executable Python projects.

- • We integrate our benchmark with the general-purpose dynamic analysis framework DynaPyt, so arbitrary dynamic analyses can be performed on the whole benchmark with minimal effort.

- • We show the usefulness of DyPyBench in three application scenarios.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Python has grown rapidly in recent years to become one of the most used programming languages in a variety of fields, including machine learning, data analysis, and web applications. For example, a 2022 report on programming languages used in projects hosted on GitHub lists Python as the second-most popular of all languages. The success of Python can be attributed to its simplicity, flexibility, and large collection of libraries and frameworks. Python's dynamic nature, which allows for dynamic type checking and modifying object structures at runtime, further adds to its appeal for developers.

The dynamic nature of Python also creates challenges for program analysis, error detection, security assessment, and performance optimization. Various dynamic program analysis techniques have been developed to address these challenges, e.g., to detect bugs [1], to enforce differential privacy [2], to slice programs [3], or to understand the performance of a program via profiling [4]. These techniques play an important role in identifying programming errors, security vulnerabilities, and performance bottlenecks. To help develop, evaluate, and compare dynamic analysis techniques, other popular programming languages have benchmark suites of executable code. For example, DaCapo for Java [5], SPEC CPU for C/C++ [6], and Da Capo con Scala [7] have contributed significantly to the work of both researchers and practitioners on their respective languages.

Despite the popularity and importance of Python, there currently is no equivalent benchmark suite for Python, which hinders the progress and evaluation of dynamic analyses. Instead, researchers who want to work on a new dynamic program analysis for Python, want to study the runtime behavior of Python code, or want to gather data from executions of Python software must spend significant effort on creating a suitable set of executable programs. As a result, many evaluations involving dynamic analysis of Python are performed on a relatively small set of benchmark programs, e.g., nine projects [8], five projects [9], six projects [10], and eleven projects [1]. Moreover, since every team working on Python creates its own benchmark, it is difficult to compare different techniques and results with each other.

In response to this gap, this paper presents DyPyBench, a novel benchmark of executable Python projects. We envision our benchmark to facilitate future work on dynamically analyzing Python. To this end, the benchmark is the first to offer four important properties – large-scale, diverse, ready-to-run, and ready-to-analyze – as described below:

- • Large-scale. To offer users an extensive collection of executable code, the benchmark includes a substantial number of popular and non-trivial projects. What counts as "large-scale" may vary depending on the specific use case. In this work, we have curated a dataset of 50 projects, amounting to 681k lines of code in total. This is an order of magnitude larger than the benchmarks considered in previous evaluations, as listed above.

- • Diverse. Given Python's numerous applications, it is critical that a benchmark covers many application domains, each of which has its own code style and libraries. DyPyBench attempts to represent the breadth and diversity of Python usage by including projects systematically sampled from different application domains, enabling extensive assessments and studies of code behavior across different contexts.

- • Ready-to-run. Executing the code of a real-world, complex project is non-trivial, as it requires a suitable project configuration, installed third-party dependencies, and inputs that exercise the code. The effort of setting up projects can be significant, especially for users unfamiliar with the project, and this effort usually has to be spent again for each new project. DyPyBench comes with all projects already set up and uses the projects' test suites to provide inputs. To make it easy to run the code regardless of differences in project dependencies, configurations, and execution environments, DyPyBench provides a unified interface that lets users run the benchmark with a single command. Moreover, we provide a Docker image that contains the benchmark and all its dependencies, ensuring reproducibility and longevity.

- • Ready-to-analyze. To facilitate the dynamic analysis of the projects in DyPyBench, the benchmark integrates with DynaPyt [8], a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework for Python. This integration allows for instrumenting and analyzing projects with a single command, making it straightforward to apply a new dynamic analysis to a wide range of projects.

To evaluate the usefulness and practicality of DyPyBench, we perform a series of experiments covering a wide range of research areas. In particular, we apply our benchmark in three usage scenarios:

- (1) We use DyPyBench to empirically compare statically and dynamically created call graphs. For this, we use the dynamic analysis infrastructure built into DyPyBench to gather dynamic call graphs and compare them to the results of a state of the art static call graph generator [11]. Our results help understand the strengths and weaknesses of both approaches and provide some guidelines for future work on call graph construction.

- (2) We use DyPyBench to create training data for LExecutor [9], a recent neural network-based technique for learning-guided execution. In this scenario, we apply the existing source code instrumentation tool of LExecutor to the code in DyPyBench and then execute our benchmark. Using the resulting 436,355 data examples as training data for the LExecutor model, we find that more data helps improve the model's accuracy.

- (3) Finally, we use DyPyBench to mine specifications from execution traces. For this application, we again build on the dynamic analysis support built into our benchmark, this time to extract traces of function calls. DyPyBench provided thousands of call sequences from which some meaningful patterns could be extracted, setting a baseline for future work on dynamic specification mining for Python.

For all three of these applications, one would usually have to spend significant effort on setting up suitable projects and finding inputs, e.g., test suites, to exercise their code. DyPyBench instead provides this setup, which greatly facilitates these and future dynamic analyses for Python.

In summary our work contributes the following:

- • We address the lack of a comprehensive benchmark suite of executable Python projects by creating DyPyBench.

- • We integrate our benchmark with the general-purpose dynamic analysis framework DynaPyt [8], which allows for performing arbitrary dynamic analyses on the entire benchmark with minimal effort.

- • We illustrate the usefulness of DyPyBench in three application scenarios.
